glosses: to be (have a temporary or permanent location in space)
to be (denotes a copula, in a transient fashion)
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Spanish estar, from Latin stō, stare.
The preterite's origin is unclear, most likely generalized from the preterite of haber (“to have”), hub- (note that b and v are pronounced identically; compare the same development in andar and tener and Portuguese estar). Preterite, imperfect subjunctive and future subjunctive forms are derived from tener. Related to English state, stand.

glosses: to have; to possess; to be (a condition or quality)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish tener (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre, teneō (“to hold; to keep; to have”), from Proto-Italic *tenēō, stative from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch or draw”). The preterite forms in tuv- are from contamination with those of the nearly synonymous haber, hub-.

ancestors.gloss: to hold; to keep; to have

glosses: to be (in the passive voice sense)
verbs.etymology_text:
From Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse. The form sois pl (“you are”) derives from a Vulgar Latin *sutis.
Along the way, the verb absorbed Old Spanish seer < Latin sedēre (“sit”). The present subjunctive may either be from the latter verb (Latin sedeām > Old Spanish *seya > modern Spanish sea) or from esse's present subjunctive extended with the Latin third conjugation present subjunctive endings (Latin sī- + -ām = *sīām > modern Spanish sea).

glosses: to go (away from speaker and listener)
to be suitable or apt for its purpose, to match or suit well (of clothing)
to head towards or lead to a place away from the speaker
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin īre (“to go”). Forms beginning with /b/ such as voy (“I go”) are inherited from Latin vādere (“to go”). Forms beginning with /f/ such as fui (“I went”) are inherited from Latin esse (“to be”), which are a result of suppletion with ser (“to be”). The imperative voseo form, andá, is a result of suppletion with andar (“to walk”).

glosses: to be familiar with something, or with someone's personality
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

glosses: to desire, to want, to want to
to love; to be fond of (usually used with people or personified objects)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin quaerō (“seek, look for, desire”). Cognate with English query.

glosses: to do, perform, execute, carry out
in various expressions about the weather
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Spanish fazer, from Latin facere.
The first-person indicative (hago) and present subjunctive forms (haga, hagas, etc.) may have been influenced by Latin agō (compare English gesture), but more likely come from a voicing of intervocalic Latin /k/ after having dropped /i/ (e.g. Latin faciō > [ˈfa.ko] > hago).

glosses: to say, to tell, to name, to mention
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish dezir, from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).

glosses: to have; forms the perfect aspect
to exist; there be; “there is”, “there are” (hay); “there was”, “there were” (hubo/había)
verbs.etymology_text:
Latinised respelling of Old Spanish aver, from Latin habēre, habeō (“have, hold”), probably from Proto-Italic *habēō or *haβēō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”). Cognate with French avoir, Italian avere, Occitan aver, Portuguese haver, Romanian avea, avere, and Sardinian (Campidanese airi, Logudorese àere).
The preterite is from metathesis of the Latin perfect habuī > *haubī.

glosses: to see, to look at, to view (perceive)
to see, to tell, to observe
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish veer, from Latin vidēre. Cognate with English view, wit, wise. Compare the borrowed doublet video.

glosses: to think, to believe, to reckon, to be of the opinion
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish creer, from Latin crēdere.

glosses: must, need to, have to (indicates an obligation or requirement)
must (used to indicate that something is likely)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish dever, from Latin dēbēre (“owe”). Cognates include English due and debt.
Inherited from Old Spanish dar (“to give”), from Latin dare.

glosses: to know how to do something
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Latin sapiō, sapere (“taste, know”). Compare English savvy, savor.
The 1SG reflects an original */ˈsajo/, in common with other Romance languages, of uncertain origin. The present subjunctive forms show consonant metathesis (sapiām > */ˈsajpa/ > Sp. sepa).

glosses: to talk; to speak; to communicate using words
to talk or speak regularly with someone, sometimes online
verbs.etymology_text: From Old Spanish fablar, from Latin fābulārī (“chat, converse”). Doublet of fabular, which was borrowed from Latin.

glosses: to think of, think that (have an opinion on)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish pensar, from Latin pēnsāre (possibly semi-learned in this form). Doublet of pesar. Compare English pensive.

glosses: to leave, to keep (to allow to continue)
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Spanish dexar, from Early Old Spanish lexar, from Latin laxāre, whence also laxar (a borrowed doublet). Also compare Portuguese and Galician deixar, Asturian dexar, Aragonese deixar, Catalan deixar, Occitan daissar, laissar, Sicilian dassari and both French laisser and délaisser.
Early Old Spanish generally has l-, forms appearing with d- towards 1200. The change of the initial l- to d- in many (especially Iberian) Romance languages has been explained in various ways: most likely, it is due to the influence of the preposition de, often used in constructions with this verb, or from an influence of, or contraction of, Late Latin dēlaxāre (also attested in Old Spanish as delexar), due to rapid pronunciation (as is common in quasi-auxiliary verbs). Less likely explanations include influence from the verb dar (“to give”), or derivation from Latin dēsinere, the latter proving difficult on phonetic grounds. Compare English lease (sense 5), lax, and laxative.
Inherited from Old Spanish venir, from Latin veniō. Cognate with Ladino venir.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin necessitō (“to oblige, compel”), from Latin necessitās (“necessity, compulsion”) + -ō (denomimal verbal suffix). According to Coromines and Pascual, attested by the 17th century. Cognate of French nécessiter, which is known to be attested much earlier.

Inherited from Old Spanish levar, from Latin levāre. The initial /ʎ/ developed from an earlier /lj/ in root-stressed conjugations such as lieva (< Latin lĕvat), where it resulted from the diphthongization of stressed Latin short ĕ to /je/. Eventually /ʎ-/ spread to the entire verb paradigm by analogy.

glosses: to pass, to hand, to slip
to pass, to get past, to go past, to go by, to go over, to get through
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish passar, from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun). Compare English pass.

glosses: to return, to revert, to get back
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin volvere (“roll, roll back”).

glosses: translated as "to like", analyzable in structure as "to please" [with dative ‘someone’] (the thing being liked is the subject, while the "liker" is in the dative case ("indirect object")). See the usage notes for more. Compare similar structures in Italian piacere, Romanian plăcea, German gefallen and Russian нравиться (nravitʹsja).
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed in this form from Latin gustāre. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form gostar. See gusto. The use of this verb to mean "like" is a uniquely Ibero-Romance development. Compare Portuguese gostar.

glosses: to look like, to seem like
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.
From Old Spanish esperar, from Latin spērō, -āre (“to hope, await”).
From Latin in contra. Compare Portuguese encontrar, Italian incontrare, and French rencontrer.

glosses: to regret, feel or be sorry
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish sentir (“to feel”), from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”). Cognate with English scent.

glosses: to put, to place (cause to assume a specified position)
to type (with a keyboard, etc.), (with a dative object) to send
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin pōnere (whence English post and position), from Proto-Italic *pozinō. Compare Portuguese pôr and Romanian pune.
Inherited from Old Spanish clamar, from Latin clāmāre (“to cry out”). Doublet of clamar, a borrowing from Latin. Cognate with English claim and clamor.

glosses: to set, to establish, to lay
to sit down, have a seat
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sedentāre, from Latin sedēns, present participle of sedeō.

glosses: to know (a person or a place), to be familiar with, to be acquainted with
to get to know, become acquainted (with)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Late Latin conōscere, variant of Latin cognōscere. Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form coñocer.

glosses: to continue (on); to keep, to keep on (can be combined with the gerund to indicate that someone or something continues doing something)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sequīre, from deponent Classical Latin sequī, sequor, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Cognate with English segue, suit, sequel, sequence, and sue.

glosses: to be (as a result of something), to end up
to be situated; to be located (used with only static objects, such as buildings)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish quedar, from Vulgar Latin *quētāre, from Late Latin quiētō, -āre. Doublet of learned quietar and semi-learned quitar. Cognate with English quit and quiet.

glosses: to go out, to leave, to depart, to head out
to go out, to come out (to leave one's abode to go to public places)
to come out (e.g. from hiding), to come off (e.g. off the bench in a sport; off of a high place like a roof or ladder)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish salir, from Latin salīre. Compare Portuguese sair and Romanian sări. Cognate with English sally. Displaced in meaning by the doublet saltar.

glosses: to get up to, to go up to, to reach (+ a or + hasta)
to be sufficient; to be enough
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin applicāre (“to land, to reach the coast”), due to the strong naval tradition in Iberian peninsula. Compare Portuguese chegar, Asturian allegar, also Romanian pleca (“to leave”), though the latter might be associated with folding up tents and leaving (see Latin plicāre).

ancestors.gloss: to land, to reach the coast

verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish ayudar, from Latin adiūtāre. Cognate with Asturian ayudar, Catalan ajudar, Ladino ayudar, Occitan ajudar, and Portuguese ajudar.

glosses: to take (put under one's physical or mental control, often in one's hands)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish tomar, of unknown origin.

glosses: to put out, extinguish (a flame or light)
verbs.etymology_text:
Several possibilities:
* From Latin mactāre (through a Vulgar Latin *mattāre). Thus, a potential cognate with English mactate.
* From Vulgar Latin *mattāre, from Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), related to madidus. Compare Portuguese and Catalan matar, archaic Italian mattare.
* From Spanish mazar, in turn from maza (“mace, club”); compare Italian ammazzare (“to kill”).
* From Arabic مَاتَ (māta, “to die”), compare Persian مات (mât), the probable source of the second part of English checkmate.

glosses: to be queer; to bat for the other team
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish entender (“to fathom”), from Latin intendere, from in- + tendō. Doublet of intender, a borrowing.

glosses: to work in, work on, to workshop (+ en)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish trabajar, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”).

glosses: to look at (to try to see, to pay attention to with one’s eyes)
to watch (to look at, view, or observe for a period of time)
to watch (to mind, attend, or guard)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish mirar, from Latin mīrārī (“marvel at”). Compare Ladino mirar (“look at”), Portuguese mirar (“see, aim”), dated French mirer (“stare”).

glosses: to end, to flow into something (a road, river, etc.)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish murir, morir, from Latin morīrī, variant of morī. Cognate with Galician morrer, Ladino murir, and Portuguese morrer. Compare English mortify.

glosses: to seek, search for, look for, try to find, to scour
to look up (in a search engine, dictionary, etc.)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish buscar. Ultimate origin unknown, possibly cognate with bosque, cognate with Portuguese buscar. Or possibly from a Celtic language; compare Old Irish búaid (“victory”) and Welsh budd (“gain”), all from Proto-Celtic *boudi (“gain”).

glosses: to listen to, to hear out
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish escuchar, ascuchar, from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of auscultar, a borrowing from Latin.

glosses: to matter, to be important [with a ‘someone’] (often translated idiomatically with English care or mind, with subject and object reversed)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin importāre.

glosses: to try, to attempt; especially: to strain or put forth effort in so doing
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin intentāre.
Inherited from Old Spanish perder, inherited from Latin perdere, whence also English perdition.

glosses: to enter; to come in; to get in; to go in; to get inside; to come on in
to join; to enter; to start
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish entrar, from Latin intrāre. Cognate with English enter.

glosses: to request someone else to do something
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere (“ask, request”). Compare English petition.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. By surface analysis, a- + cabo (“end, conclusion”) + -ar.

glosses: to start, begin, to get started
verbs.etymology_text: From en- + pieza + -ar. The underlying meanings is "to start", to consume something by breaking off a "piece" or by breaking it open.

glosses: to suppose, to surmise, to assume, to guess, to imagine, to figure, to say, to take it
to pose (e.g. a risk, a threat, a danger)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin supponere. Cognate with English suppose.

glosses: to wonder, to ask oneself, to ponder
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish preguntar, from Vulgar Latin *praecūnctāre, alteration of Latin percontārī.

glosses: to bring (in the sense of transport, for differences with llevar and examples see that entry)
to make (cause to be in or have a certain condition or state)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish traer, from Latin trahō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ-.

glosses: to achieve, succeed in, reach, accomplish, attain
to get, obtain, acquire, find, gain, procure, extract, get to
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish conseguir, from Vulgar Latin *cōnsequiō or *cōnsequō, from Latin cōnsequor.
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre.
From Old Spanish recordar, from Latin recordārī. Cognate with English record.

glosses: to worry, to concern, to trouble, to be worrisome to, to preoccupy
to care, to worry, to be concerned, to be troubled
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupāre (“to preoccupy”). Cognate with English preoccupy.

glosses: to treat (to handle, behave toward in a specific way)
to treat (to submit to a chemical action)
verbs.etymology_text: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin tractāre (“to drag; to handle; to practice”), from tractus (“dragged”), perfect passive participle of trahō (“to drag; to extract”). Cf. also the obsolete or regional inherited doublet trechar (“to cut open and salt eels being dried and cured”). Cognate to English treat and Portuguese tratar.

ancestors.gloss: to drag; to handle; to practice

glosses: to (cause to) finish, to (cause to) end, to (cause to) terminate, to (cause to) conclude
to finish, to end, to terminate, to be over, to conclude (of a thing)
to end up, to wind up, to turn out
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin termināre.

glosses: [with le] to elude, to escape, to slip someone's mind (be forgotten by)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish olbidar, olvidar, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, frequentative of Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus).
Borrowed from Latin creāre. Compare the inherited doublet criar (“to raise”).

glosses: to change, to shift, to switch, to alter
to switch, to switch up, to change, to trade, to swap (usually + de) (when implying changing from one thing to another)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre, of Gaulish origin. Probably through Asturian cambiar, Galician cambiar or Aragonese cambiar, given the conservation of mb group. Compare also the probable native variant Old Spanish form camear. Cognate to Italian cambiare.

glosses: to put out, to get out (e.g. a public statement, an APB, a release of media or entertainment)
to pull out, to take out (e.g. a badge, an ID card, a picture, paperwork, the keys, finger)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish sacar (in Cantar de mio Cid), perhaps from Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌺𐌰𐌽 (sakan, “to dispute, to rebuke”). Cognate with English seek, sake, Latin sāgiō.

glosses: to sustain, to preserve, to retain, to uphold
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Equivalent to mano + tener. Compare Galician and Portuguese manter, French maintenir, Italian mantenere.

glosses: to listen to (actively pay attention to a sound or a person speaking)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish oir, from Latin audīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”). Compare French ouïr, Italian udire, Portuguese ouvir, and Romanian auzi.

glosses: to make a living, to live on
verbs.etymology_text: From Old Spanish bevir, bivir, vevir, viver, inherited from Latin vīvere. Compare Ladino bivir, Portuguese viver.
Inherited from Old Spanish dormir, from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.
Borrowed from Latin significāre.

glosses: to be (a certain number of years of age)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin computāre. Doublet of computar. Cognate with English count and compute.

glosses: to happen, to befall, to occur
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin succēdere. The meaning of "to be successful" was lost from this verb and given to the verb conseguir and the verb phrase "tener éxito".

Inherited from Old Spanish jogar, from Latin iocor, from iocus (“joke, jest”) + -ō (denominal verbal suffix). The shift from /o/ to /u/ is irregular and produced the only verb with u-ue vowel alternation in Spanish.
Cognate with Asturian xugar, Catalan jugar, French jouer, Galician xogar, Italian giocare, Portuguese jogar, Romanian juca, and, more distantly, English joke.

glosses: to return, go back, come back
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin regressus, from re- + gressus; cognate with English regress.

glosses: to move (to cause to change place or posture)
to shake (e.g. to shake one's head, to shake one's tail feather)
to wiggle (e.g. one's ears, fingers, nose, toes)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish mover, from Latin movēre. Cognate with English move.
Inherited from Old Spanish ganar, from Early Medieval Latin ganāre, q.v.

glosses: to buy (to obtain in exchange of money or goods)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”), whence also Portuguese comprar, Italian comprare, Romanian cumpăra.
From función + -ar.

glosses: to be worthwhile, to have a pay off
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish pagar, from Latin pācāre (“to pacify”), from pāx (“peace”, whence paz) + -āre (denominative verbal suffix)
Borrowed from Latin occurrere (“appear, occur”), from ob + currō (“run”).
Inherited from Late Latin inviāre, which is derived from Latin via (“path, road”). Compare Portuguese enviar, French envoyer, Italian inviare.
Inherited from Old Spanish leer, from Latin legēre (“to collect, gather; to read”). Cognate with English legend, legible, lesson.

glosses: to throw, toss, cast, jettison (to release an object from one's grasp so that it moves through the air)
to pour (to cause to flow in a stream from a container)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish echar, from Early Medieval Latin iectāre, from Classical Latin iactāre. Doublet of the borrowing jactar. Cognate with Catalan gitar, Galician xeitar, French jeter, Portuguese jeito, and Sicilian jittari; alongside more distantly English jet and jut.

glosses: to welcome, to greet, to receive (guests, patients)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin recipere.

glosses: to shoot, to fire (e.g. a weapon, a rocket)
to rise, to go up, to skyrocket
to go off, to be suddenly jolted into action
verbs.etymology_text: Latinizing alteration of Old Spanish desparar, from Latin disparāre (“separate”), from dis- + parō (“make equal”), although it was taken as the negative of parō (“prepare, arrange”) in Romance.

glosses: to write (to form letters, words or symbols on a surface in order to communicate)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish escrivir, from Vulgar Latin *scrībīre, from Latin scrībere.
Inherited from Late Latin perdōnāre.

Inherited from Old Spanish començar, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, from com- + Latin initiāre. Did not show diphthongized conjugations in early medieval texts; their later appearance seems to reflect analogy with the synonym empezar.
Borrowed from Latin permittere.

Inherited from Old Spanish meter, from Latin mittere (“to send”). The semantic shift from "send" to "put" probably occurred in Vulgar Latin.
Cognate with English mess and also mission, message. Compare also French mettre, Friulian meti, Portuguese meter, and Italian mettere.
Possibly a semi-learned borrowing from Latin incantāre. By surface analysis, en- + cantar.
Inherited from Old Spanish comer, from Vulgar Latin *comēre, restructuring of Latin comedere.

glosses: to marry, wed someone to (unite two others in wedlock)
verbs.etymology_text:
Probably from casa + -ar (lit. "to become a member of the house"). Compare also Italian accasare, Romanian căsători.

Derived from Latin cassāre.
Borrowed from Latin dētinēre. Cognate with English detain, Italian detenere, Portuguese deter, and Romanian deține.
Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin aperīre. Compare English apricate.

glosses: to go up or come up
verbs.etymology_text: From Old Spanish subir (borrowed, inherited form sobir), from Latin subīre (“approach”).

glosses: to take, catch, hold, to get, to seize
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Latin colligere (“to collect, to gather”). Cognate with Portuguese colher, French cueillir, Sicilian cògghiri, and also with English cull, coil, college, and collect. Compare also the borrowed doublet colegir.
Not related to Latin cōgere, coagere (“to assemble”).
Inherited from Old Spanish salvar, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus. Compare French sauver, Italian salvare.

glosses: to accept, to take up, to take up on
verbs.etymology_text: Re-Latinized from Old Spanish acetar, from Latin acceptāre. Cognate with English accept.
Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre. Cognate with English muster, Italian mostrare, Occitan muishar and French montrer.
Inherited from Old Spanish prometer, from Latin prōmittere (“to promise; to send forth”).
From Latin *confidare, from cōnfīdēre.

glosses: to turn into, to cause to become
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin convertō.

glosses: to look after, take care of (e.g. a house, a person)
to mind, watch, pay attention to, be mindful of
to look after oneself, take care
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Spanish cuidar (“to think; to take care of”), from Latin cogitāre (“to think”).
Doublet of cogitar, a learned borrowing from Latin, whence also English cogitate.

glosses: to shoo, chase away, drive away
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish correr, from Latin currere.

glosses: to learn (to acquire, or attempt to acquire knowledge or an ability to do something)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish aprender, from Latin apprēndere, from earlier apprehendere. Doublet of aprehender, a borrowing. Cognate with English apprehend.

glosses: to fall (to move to a lower position due to gravity)
to fall (to come down, to drop, to descend)
to fall down, to collapse (to fall to the ground)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish caer, from Late Latin cadēre, from Classical Latin cadere. Cognate with French choir, Galician caer, Portuguese cair.
From Latin imāginārī, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

glosses: to serve (to be a servant or worker; to render service)
to serve (to be a servant for; to work for)
to be of use, to be good for
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin servīre.

glosses: to ring a bell, to be familiar
verbs.etymology_text: From Old Spanish sonar, inherited from Latin sonō, -āre.

glosses: to draw (e.g., a card from an opponent in a game)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Late Latin raubāre.

glosses: to put up; to build up (buildings)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish levantar, either from levante (corresponding to Latin levāntem), the old present participle of levar, itself the Old Spanish form of llevar, from Latin levō, levāre, or from a Vulgar Latin *levantāre, derived from levāns, levānte-, present participle of levō. Compare Galician and Portuguese levantar, Asturian llevantar, Romansh alvantar, leventar.

glosses: to be someone's time or turn, or time to do something
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *toccāre, *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.

From toca (“headscarf, wimple, kind of hat”).

glosses: to sell for (a sum), to fetch
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin vēndere (“to sell”).

glosses: to remove, to take away, to take down, to take off, to pull off, to pull out, to clear, to clear away, to strip, to strip away
verbs.etymology_text: Probably a semi-learned derivation from Medieval Latin quitāre (“release, discharge, set free”) from Late Latin quietāre, or from Latin quietus (through an Old Spanish adjective quito, with an abnormal phonological evolution). Compare English quiet and quit and French quitter. See also Spanish quedar and quietar.

glosses: to secure (to make fast; to close or confine effectually)
to assure (to give (someone) confidence in the trustworthiness of)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish assegurar, from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrare, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”). Compare English assure.

glosses: to break up, terminate (a relationship, friendship etc.)
to begin to do something; to break into
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish romper, from Latin rumpō, rumpere (“to break”).

glosses: to desire, to want, to hope for, to long for
verbs.etymology_text: From the noun deseo; cf. Latin dēsīderō, dēsīderāre (“long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin verb *dēsidiāre, itself perhaps a crossing between Latin dēsīderāre and invidiāre, from invidia. Compare Portuguese desejar, Catalan desitjar.

glosses: to decide, to make up one's mind, to determine, to choose to
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin decidere.
Borrowed from Latin praeparāre (“to prepare”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (found also in Medieval Latin, per Du Cange), from Latin signāre.
From alegre + -ar.

glosses: to shut down, to close down
to turn off, to shut off (to rotate a tap or valve so as to interrupt the outflow of liquid or gas)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Vulgar Latin serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”). Compare English serry/serried.
Borrowed from Latin explicāre.

glosses: to get off, to get down, to climb down, to step down, to get out (e.g., of/from a platform or vehicle)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish baxar, from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre, from Late Latin bassus.

glosses: to put something in a vertical position
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish parar, from Latin parō.
Inherited from Old Spanish mentir (“to lie”), from Latin mentīrī.

glosses: to show; to show signs of
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin praesentāre.
Learned borrowing from Latin referō.

glosses: to fix, to repair, to mend
to settle, to sort, to sort out, to patch up, to solve
to straighten out, to fix up, to tidy, to tidy up, to clean up
verbs.etymology_text: From a- + regla + -ar.
Inherited from Old Spanish provar, from Latin probāre.
From disculpa (“apology, excuse”) + -ar.
From Latin existere, infinitive of existō.
Inherited from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Equivalent to des- + cubrir.

glosses: to love, have great affection for, care about
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish amar, from Latin amāre.
Borrowed from Latin protegere.
Inherited from Latin plōrāre (“cry out”). Compare English implore.

glosses: to run away, get away, slip away, flee
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish escapar, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, from Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

glosses: to throw out, to toss, to dump
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

glosses: to talk back, to answer back (to respond defiantly and inappropriately)
to respond, to react (to someone else's actions)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish responder, inherited from Latin respondēre (likely via Late Latin respondĕre). The original past participle was respuso or repuso in Old Spanish. The expected diphthongization of stressed Latin /ŏ/ is found in Asturian responder (that is, respuendo) and sporadically in Old Spanish as well.

glosses: to appear, to turn up, to pop up, to come up
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish aparecer, from Late Latin apparescō, from Latin appāreō + -scō (inchoative suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, camino + -ar.

glosses: to be afraid, sorry; to suspect
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin timēre.

glosses: to go off on, to go off of (idiomatic)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin continuāre.

Borrowed from Old Occitan balar, from Late Latin ballāre, borrowed from, or related to, Ancient Greek βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”). Doublet of inherited ballar. Compare French baller, Italian ballare, English ballet.
From Latin condūcere (“lead, bring or draw together”), from con- + dūcō (“lead”). Cognate with English conduce.

glosses: to be accustomed to doing something, to do something on a regular basis, to do something usually or often
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish soler (“to use to”), from Latin solēre. Compare Catalan soler, Italian solere, Ladino soler and Portuguese soer (archaic).

glosses: to bother, to disturb, to trouble, to impose, to inconvenience, to burden
to annoy, to tease, to pester, to bug, to hassle
verbs.etymology_text: Learned borrowing from Latin molestāre (“to bother”), from molestus (“troublesome”).

glosses: to hit, to knock, to tap
verbs.etymology_text: From golpe + -ear.
Borrowed from Latin praeferre, with a change of conjugation. Cognate with English prefer.
Inherited from Old Spanish elegir, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin ēligere. Compare the inherited form esleer ~ esleír.

glosses: to approach, to get close, to come
verbs.etymology_text: From a- + cerca (“near”) + -ar. Compare Ladino aserkar and Portuguese acercar.

glosses: to achieve, to manage to, to pull off
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin lucrārī. Doublet of lucrar.

glosses: to disappear, to go missing, to vanish, to be gone
to drop off (e.g. the map, the face of the earth)
to go away, to fade, to wear off, to subside
verbs.etymology_text: From des- + aparecer.
Borrowed from Latin obtinēre, with conjugation based on tener.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin āctuāre (“actuate”), from Latin āctus, perfect passive participle of agō (“do, act”).

glosses: to find out, figure out, work out, determine
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish averiguar, from Late Latin vērificāre as a semi-learned term, with the prefix a- from Latin ad-. According to Coromines and Pascual, citing Rufino José Cuervo, it is first attested in a Fuero Juzgo from 1240.

glosses: to offer, to offer up, to provide
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish ofresçer, derived from ofrir, from Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.

glosses: to return, refund, restore, give back, hand back, bring back, send back etc.
to pay back, repay (to pay an amount of money owed to another)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin dēvolvere (“roll or tumble off or down”). Cognate with English devolve.

ancestors.gloss: roll or tumble off or down

glosses: to fight, to battle, to do battle
to struggle, to strive, to contend, to grapple
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin luctārī. Compare Portuguese lutar, French lutter

glosses: to have sex, used especially when talking about a nubile girl
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *merēscere, from Latin merēre.
Inherited from Old Spanish, inherited from Latin comprendere, variant of comprehendere. Cognate with English comprehend.
Borrowed from Latin recuperāre, from earlier reciperāre. Doublet of recobrar, which was inherited.

glosses: to fight (to contend in physical conflict)
to fight for, to struggle against
verbs.etymology_text: From pelo (“hair”) + -ear, in the sense of close physical combat, as in the expression agarrarse de las greñas (“to fight”, literally “to grab each others' matted locks”). Compare the semantic development of Romanian părui (“to fight by pulling hair”) from Romanian păr (“hair”).

glosses: to collect, to gather, to pick up, to fetch, to retrieve (something previously left behind)
to pick up (a person or people by vehicle)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin recolligere. Doublet of recolegir, a borrowing. Compare English recollect.
Borrowed from French attraper, ultimately from Germanic. More at English trap.
Inherited from Latin volāre. Doublet of volear. Compare Galician and Portuguese voar.
From odio + -ar and/or Latin odi.

Inherited from Old Spanish esconder, from an original asconder (with a replacement of the prefix with es-), from Latin abscondere. It formerly showed the expected diphthongization of stressed short Latin /o/ in rhizotonic conjugations (see older escuendo), but this was later levelled out by analogy with arrhizotonic conjugations.
Doublet of absconder and cognate with English abscond.

Inherited from Old Spanish soltar, from a Vulgar Latin *soltāre (a root), from *solutāre, as a frequentative of Latin solvere. Equivalent to suelto + -ar (with -ue- becoming -o- due to destressing of that syllable).
Borrowed from French marcher. Compare Catalan marxar.

glosses: to avoid, to bypass, to evade, to circumvent, to dodge, to shun, to eschew (to steer clear of)
to avoid, to prevent, to keep from, to stop from, to avert, to obviate, to deter
to help (abstain from doing) (always in the negative)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin ēvītāre whence English inevitable.

glosses: to cut off, cut out, cut through, cut down, cut up, to nip
to chop, chop up, chop off
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin curtāre (“shorten”). Compare English curtail.

glosses: to joke, to kid (to do or say something for amusement)
verbs.etymology_text: From broma + -ear.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rīdīre (with dissimilation?), from Latin rīdēre. The perfect system and past participle were changed; the expected preterite indicative would be *rese or *rise with the expected past participle being *reso or *riso.
Inherited from Old Spanish agradesçer, equivalent to a- + grado (“will; liking, preference”) + -ecer. Cognate with Aragonese agradeixer and Catalan agrair.

glosses: to calm, to still (to limit and lessen in motion and disturbance)
to calm, soothe, assuage, to ease, to appease, to quell, to allay, to settle, to relieve (to make lessen in intensity)
to defuse (e.g. a situation or problem, tension or conflict, a crisis)
verbs.etymology_text: From calma + -ar.
Borrowed from Latin dīrigere.

glosses: to occupy (to take or use space)
to occupy (to fill or hold a position)
to occupy, to take up (time or space)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin occupāre. Cognate with English occupy.
A learned formation stemming from Latin revīsus (may also be seen as a compound of re- + visar). Compare French réviser; cf. also Latin reviso, revisere.
Inherited from Old Spanish destruir, a learned borrowing from Latin dēstruō.

glosses: to scare, to frighten, to spook
to freak out (somebody), to creep out
verbs.etymology_text: Either derived from a- + susto (“fright”) + -ar, or less likely from a Latin suscitāre (which would hypothetically make it a cognate with English suscitate). More likely linked to Latin substāre, from sub- + stō . Compare Portuguese assustar.

glosses: to result, to turn out, to end up, to prove
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin resultāre.
From Latin dis- (“apart, separate”) + Spanish fruto (“fruit”) + -ar. Naively – "to separate the fruit" (from the plant). Cognate with Portuguese desfrutar [from 18th c.]

Inherited from Old Spanish cresçer, from Latin crēscĕre, from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”). Compare French croître, Italian crescere and English crescent.

glosses: to lead, be in charge, command
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish mandar, from Latin mandāre, present active indicative of mandō (“order, commission”).

glosses: to manage, to handle (e.g. managing symptoms, pain, stress or emotions)
to monitor, to check, to supervise, to oversee, to verify, to regulate, to check on
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from French contrôler.
Borrowed from Italian attaccare.

glosses: to trick, to deceive, to hoodwink, to cheat
to cheat on, to be unfaithful to one's spouse
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō. Compare Portuguese enganar, Catalan enganyar,
Romanian îngâna,
Italian ingannare. Cf. also Medieval Latin (in)gannatura (“mockery”).

glosses: to shout, to scream, to cry out, to call out
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.
From Latin divertere (“to turn away; to separate”). Compare English divert.

glosses: to hurt (to cause physical or emotional pain)
to grieve, regret something; to feel sorry about
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish doler, inherited from Latin dolēre, doleō, from Proto-Italic *doleō (“hurt, cause pain”), from Proto-Indo-European *dolh₁éyeti (“divide”), from *delh₁- (“cut”). Compare English condolence.

glosses: to flush, to make flush, to level
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accordāre.

glosses: to use; to make use of; to utilize
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from French utiliser, which is from Italian utilizzare. By surface analysis, útil + -izar.

glosses: to pry into, investigate (make inquiries where one is not welcome)
to smell out, uncover (find out by prying)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish oler, from Latin oleō. Cognate with English olfactor and odor.
Borrowed from Italian maneggiare. Displaced the older Spanish manear, itself of the same origin (Vulgar Latin *manizāre). Compare English manage.

glosses: to save (to store for future use)
to save (to write a file to disk or other storage medium)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.

From despierto (“awake”) + -ar, or it may correspond to a Vulgar Latin *expertāre, from *expertus, from Latin experrēctus (“awoken”), perfect passive participle of expergīscor (“to awake, to wake up”). Cognate with Galician despertar, espertar, Catalan despertar, Portuguese despertar, and Walloon dispierter.
Inherited from Latin recognōscere. Cognate with English recognize.

glosses: to gather, to collect, to bring together, to assemble, to get together, to round up, to marshal, to compile, to put together, to pull together, to draw together, to pool
to satisfy, to meet, to possess (e.g. conditions, requirements, criteria, qualifications, characteristics)
verbs.etymology_text: From re- + unir.

glosses: to make out with, to neck with
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish, from Latin bāsiāre (“to kiss”).

glosses: to dine; to have supper; to have a lavish meal
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin cēnāre.
From limpio + -ar, or from Late Latin limpidāre, from Latin limpidus. Compare Portuguese and Galician limpar, Asturian llimpiar.
Borrowed from French abandonner, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną.
Borrowed from Latin ūnīre.

glosses: to remove to a distance, put farther away, to lead away, to draw away
verbs.etymology_text: From a- + lejos + -ar.

glosses: to suffer (be confronted with something undesired)
to withstand, endure, resist or undergo a physical or moral damage
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish sufrir, sofrir, from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

glosses: to handle, take care of, to deal with, to take charge of something
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre. By surface analysis, en- + cargar. Compare Italian incaricare, Portuguese encarregar.

Inherited from Old Spanish fuir~foir, from Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, fugiō, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with French fuir, Portuguese fugir, Galician fuxir, Asturian afuxir, Catalan fugir.

glosses: to deliver, to hand over, to hand off
to turn in (e.g. homework), hand in
verbs.etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Spanish entregar, entegrar, semi-learned borrowing from Latin integrāre with metathesis (compare Old Spanish entrego).
Doublet of integrar (“to integrate”) and enterar (“to inform; to find out”). Cognate with English integrate.
Inherited from Old Spanish sobrevivir, from Latin supervīvere, equivalent to sobre- + vivir.

glosses: to discuss, to argue; to talk about
to examine some subject in detail
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin discutere - discutiō.

glosses: to split, to divide (in order to share)
verbs.etymology_text: From Latin compartī, present passive infinitive of compartior.

glosses: to rest, relax (be in a state of rest or inactivity)
to rest (put into a state of rest)
verbs.etymology_text: From des- + cansar, literally “de-tire”.

glosses: to consider, to regard, to see, to look, to view
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin cōnsīderāre. Cognate with English consider.
Borrowed from Latin cōnstruere.

glosses: to be born, to sprout, to begin to grow; to hatch (out)
to grow; to rise, to have its source (river); to rise (sun); to have its roots; to arise
to feel a desire or an urge to do something without anyone asking you to
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish nasçer, from Latin nascere.
From interés + -ar (see Latin intersum).

glosses: to accompany, to go with, to join, to tag along
verbs.etymology_text: From a- + compaña + -ar.
Borrowed from Late Latin aequivocāre. Cognate with English equivocate.

glosses: to grab or take hold of
verbs.etymology_text: From a- + garra (“claw”) + -ar.
From a- + costa (“coast”) + -ar. Cognate with English accost (“to lie alongside”, obsolete definition).
Inherited from Old Spanish respirar, from Latin respīrāre. Cognate with English respire.

glosses: to find out, to learn, to come to know, to hear
verbs.etymology_text: Either from entero, or inherited from Latin integrāre (“to renew, restore, make whole”); compare doublets entregar (“to deliver”) (semi-learned) and integrar (“to make up, compose”) (a later learned borrowing). Compare English integrate.

glosses: to be silent, to shut up
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *callāre, from Latin chalāre, from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō). Compare Portuguese calar.
From a- + ruina + -ar.
From viaje + -ar or from Catalan viatjar, from viatge.
Borrowed from Latin vigilāre. See the doublet velar. Cognate with English vigilate.

glosses: to be on, to assume or take responsibility for paying
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin invītāre. Compare the doublet envidar, from the same source, and also convidar, from a variant form. Cognate with English invite.
From mención + -ar.

glosses: to resolve, sort out, settle, address, tackle, overcome, iron out
to solve, figure out, work out, crack
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish resolver, a learned borrowing from Latin resolvō, -ere. Equivalent to re- + solver. Cognate with English resolve.

Inherited from Latin pertinēre (from whence a rare older Spanish pertener), with the suffix -ecer, or possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *pertinēscēre. Compare Portuguese pertencer. Related to pertain and pertinent.

glosses: to confront, to face (can also be translated with deal with, tackle, etc.)
to pit something against something else
to pit two things against each other
verbs.etymology_text: From en- + frente + -ar.

glosses: to accept, to admit, to agree to, to concede
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin admittere.
From estudio + -ar, from Latin studium. Compare English study, Latin studeō, Portuguese estudar.

glosses: to wreak, to bring, to provoke
verbs.etymology_text: From causa + -ar. Cf. Medieval Latin causāre.

glosses: to crack up, have a laugh
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin partīre (“to distribute, divide”). Compare English party.
Borrowed from French surprendre, with conjugation based on prender. First attested in the 17th century.
Inherited from Latin negāre.
From Old Spanish espedir (“to ask to leave”), influenced by des-, from expetō (“to claim, to demand”), from petō (“to request, to seek”).

glosses: to draw from (to be inspired by)
verbs.etymology_text: From Old Spanish bever, inherited from Latin bibere. Cognate with Catalan beure, French boire, Italian bere, Portuguese beber, Romanian bea. The modern spelling with intervocalic ⟨b⟩ replacing medieval ⟨v⟩ is due to Latin influence.
Inherited from Old Spanish cubrir, cobrir, from Latin cooperīre. Cognate with English cover.

glosses: to soothe (e.g., the body, one's skin)
to loosen up, to ease up, to ease, to lighten, (e.g., a restriction, the mood)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin relaxāre. Cognate with English relax.

glosses: to depend, to be subject to
to depend on, to rely on, to hinge on, to depend upon, to rely upon
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin dēpendēre.

glosses: to fulfil, to fulfill, to meet, to deliver (e.g., requirements, prerequisites, promise, vow)
to achieve, to accomplish, to carry out, to perform, to complete, to discharge, to fulfil (e.g., one's duties, responsibilities)
to turn a certain age (may be succeeded by los)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish cumplir~complir, from Vulgar Latin *complīre, from Latin complēre. The retention of /pl/ is unusual and perhaps reflects some form of conservative tendency. Cf. henchir < *implīre < implēre for the more usual outcome. Compare also Portuguese cumprir, which shows a similar lack of palatalization.

glosses: to bear, to endure, to withstand, put up with, tolerate, to stomach, to weather, to handle
to support a weight or load
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from Latin supportāre. First attested in the fifteenth century. Cognate with English support although divergent in meaning.

glosses: to match; to fit; to go with
to be strong or bright (said of the sun or light)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Latin picāre (“smear with pitch”), derived from pix (“pitch”). Compare English pitch.
Inherited from Latin dēmōnstrāre.
From Latin vīsitāre (“to see, to visit”).

glosses: to find something, deliberately or not
to find oneself in a certain way (+adjective)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish fallar (“to find”), following internal consonant spread and palatalization, namely via Vulgar Latin *faflāre, from Latin afflāre (“to breathe or blow upon”). Cognate to Portuguese achar, Romanian afla. For the phonetic development, compare Old Spanish finchar, Spanish hinchar.
From Latin investīgāre.

glosses: to extinguish (a flame, fire), to douse
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appācāre, from Latin ad- + pācāre. Compare to English apay.
From re- + tirar. Cognate with English retire.
From Latin suggerō.
Inherited from Old Spanish cometer, from Latin committere.

glosses: to tell, tip off, notify, inform
to ask for the services of (a professional)
verbs.etymology_text: Borrowed from French aviser, from Latin advisāre. Cognate with English advise.
Inherited from Old Spanish saltar, from Latin saltāre, from saliō + -tō (forming frequentatives). Doublet of sotar, a rare regional term.

glosses: to order (request a product or service)
verbs.etymology_text: Semi-learned term derived from Latin ōrdināre. Doublet of the inherited ordeñar (“to milk”), with a specialized sense.
Borrowed from Latin contractāre, or from contrato + -ar.
Inherited from Old Spanish permanesçer, from Vulgar Latin *permanēscere, from Latin permanēre.

Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre.
The preterite's origin is unclear, most likely generalized from the preterite of haber (“to have”), hub- (note that b and v are pronounced identically; compare the same development in tener, and more alike to this verb, estar).
Borrowed from Latin contestārī (“to call to witness”).

glosses: to repeat (to do or say again (and again))
to repeat; to recur (to appear or happen again)
verbs.etymology_text: Learned borrowing from Latin repetere (“to strike back; to repeat”).
Inherited from Latin convincere.

Inherited from Latin attribuere (“associate, assign, allot, appoint”), from Latin tribuere (“grant, yield”). Doublet of atribuir (“attribute”). Compare English attribute. Also cf. Old Spanish trever, which was the normal form during the Middle Ages.
From largo.

glosses: to move, relocate, move to a new house
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Old Spanish mudar, from Latin mutāre. Doublet of the borrowed mutar. Cognate with English moult. Compare English mutate.

glosses: to hurt (in its intransitive sense, to cause physical or mental pain)
verbs.etymology_text: Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre). Doublet of blasfemar, which was borrowed from Latin.

glosses: to plane, to glide (fly unpowered, of a bird or plane)
verbs.etymology_text:
From plan + -ear.

From plano (see aeroplano) + -ear.
Borrowed from Latin observāre.
From earlier dubdar, from Latin dubitāre.
Borrowed from Latin firmāre (“make firm, confirm”). Doublet of hirmar.

glosses: to check, to check on, to check out, to see, to check to see (examine)
to verify, to ascertain, to determine, to confirm
to test (the accuracy or effectiveness of something)
